papers.title: Locating Debunkers for Rumor Mitigation in Directed Networks
papers.abstract: Rumors can spread widely through social networks, making the selection of a limited number of debunkers to disseminate corrective information important. Existing centrality-based methods only consider the individual influence of a node on spreading processes. Those individually influential nodes often have heavily overlapping influence ranges, resulting in a limited number of users they can cover. To address this problem, we propose the so-called Hybrid Marginal Influence (HMI) framework, which combines node centrality with additional audience coverage provided by each candidate and adaptively balances these two factors through a greedy selection procedure. We further develop the Debunker-Augmented SIR (DA-SIR) model for the propagation of rumors and corrective information. Experiments on ten real-world directed networks show that HMI generally selects debunkers with broader audience coverage than conventional centrality-based methods, accompanied by a lower final cumulative fraction of users who repost the rumor.

papers.title: Decisions at the end of the world
papers.abstract: International treaties are often described as tigers without teeth, failing to secure compliance or change outcomes. Cooperation also depends on how states maintain the rules they have already made -- especially where no sovereign stands above the states. Here we map more than six decades of decision-making under the Antarctic Treaty, linking submitted proposals to recorded responses and tracing how instruments act on earlier ones. Shared references tie decisions together across the agenda. Recurring revision concentrates in specialised histories, above all the management of protected areas, beyond what activity, popularity and reference age predict. Periodic administrative reviews retire outdated instruments in bulk, joining otherwise separate histories without coordinating policy across subjects. Binding Measures build overwhelmingly on earlier Measures, with little direct succession from non-binding Resolutions. Distinguishing these layers shows how a shared rule system is sustained by consensus, and provides a basis for comparing cooperation across global commons.

papers.title: Tracing dependency networks explains how origins shape downstream vulnerability
papers.abstract: Many systems sustain outcomes through chains of prerequisites, yet these dependencies are often partially observed. We trace backward from sampled outcomes to recover dependency structure and measure edge importance by the fraction of outcomes lost after an edge fails. Across 1,620 synthetic networks, revealing 90% of origins required tracing 7.24% of outcomes on average. We define pair thickness as the number of origin and outcome pairs connected through an edge. Under strict dependency, where every input is necessary, thickness counts each affected outcome once per upstream origin, whereas loss counts it once. Edges therefore form origin groups with distinct thickness and loss relations, also seen in software, citation and river topologies. Within a network, greater origin diversity corresponds to lower strict loss at equal complete thickness. We develop a growth model that predicts how edges populate these groups and how losses are distributed under partial observation, tested on 2,560 independent networks. Separating origin counts from downstream reach improves identification of edges causing the greatest losses among unsampled outcomes in strict synthetic tests. Substitutable inputs reduce losses and change which importance scores perform best. Edge importance thus measures a dependency's contribution to sustaining later outcomes, guiding the protection of critical connections.

papers.title: Inheritance of Connectivity: Modeling Higher-Order Dynamic Networks with the Birth-Death Process
papers.abstract: Higher-order networks extend pairwise interactions to represent group relationships and provide a useful framework for modeling complex systems. Understanding their dynamic evolution is important for explaining emergent structural and functional properties. However, constructing dynamic higher-order network models with stable topology remains challenging. In this paper, we propose a higher-order dynamic network model based on an inheritance-based deletion (IBAD) mechanism, which probabilistically redistributes connections when nodes or hyperedges are removed. The model combines birth-death dynamics with preferential attachment, enabling the analysis of evolving higher-order systems. Inheritance is guided by a Gaussian similarity measure based on the distance between degree histories. We derive stationary population distributions and conditional relations for connection retention and degree evolution. Simulation results show that the model generates networks with statistically stable node and hyperedge populations and heterogeneous degree distributions. The degree distributions and local clustering can be adjusted through the node and hyperedge attachment parameters. Comparisons with alternative mechanisms show that inheritance enhances connectivity relative to direct deletion, while the similarity measure influences degree heterogeneity. Comparisons with empirical networks from ecological and communication systems quantify distributional differences using Jensen-Shannon and Kullback-Leibler divergences and reveal discrepancies in clustering and within-hyperedge node-pair counts. These results provide a framework for studying population stability and structural evolution in dynamic higher-order networks.

papers.title: Scale-rich network metamaterials grow by local rules on a recursive cell division
papers.abstract: Scale-rich (SR) metamaterials are planar ligament networks grown by nucleating a segment at a random point and angle and extending it until it meets the existing structure. In the dual graph, where ligaments are nodes and junctions are links, the degree distribution has a $k^{-3}$ tail. We show that the SR construction is Cowan's iterated cell division with area-weighted selection, so the cell genealogy is a random binary search tree, and that the dual grows by a face-local rule: a new node joins two nodes on the boundary of one face. Preferential attachment on face incidences would give the Barab\'asi--Albert law, but the geometry works differently. A ligament is hit in proportion to its length, fixed at birth, and its degree is close to a Poisson variable with mean $4\ell_i(\sqrt T-\sqrt i)/c_L$, without reinforcement. Length is a fitness assigned by the cell hierarchy, $\ell_i\propto i^{-1/2}$, and the $k^{-3}$ tail follows. Integral geometry gives the probability that a new ligament cuts off a corner of its cell, which sets the triangle closure and the clustering spectrum $C(k)\simeq2p/k$. Square-closing splits raise the shortest-path multiplicity above its value at fixed degree sequence. Thickness, jamming, angle sets and density gradients leave $\gamma=3$; coherent orientation fields give $\gamma\simeq2.4$--$2.5$. For plates in three dimensions the fitness is the birth area and $\gamma=5/2$, whereas preferential attachment would give $2.44$; fluctuation tests select the fitness mechanism. The reported per-ligament energy law cannot distinguish degree from length or age.

papers.title: Persistent structural regimes in Bitcoin transactions relate to market cycles
papers.abstract: Bitcoin's blockchain is a public record of every on-chain transaction, while the price of bitcoin is set by trading on external markets. We ask whether on-chain activity alone reveals regimes associated with market trends, and whether this association remains stable over time. We summarise each week of blockchain activity from 2012 to 2026 using four measures of transaction structure and fit a two-state hidden semi-Markov model without price data. The sole market-informed constraint is an asymmetry in regime persistence, motivated by the observation that Bitcoin's price increases tend to outlast its declines. During earlier market cycles, the inferred regimes exhibit distinct transaction structures and align with periods of rising and falling prices more closely than random sequences with the same regime-duration distributions. The ongoing downturn, however, breaks this correspondence: the blockchain remains in the longer-lived regime, while its transaction structure resembles neither previous downturns nor previous upturns. Our findings support a relationship between on-chain activity and market dynamics, while highlighting its potentially time-dependent nature.

papers.title: The landscape of quantum technology companies in 2026
papers.abstract: We update our 2022 mapping of 441 quantum technology (QT) companies and examine how the industry has developed. The principal dataset now includes 1,092 companies founded with a QT focus, of which 935 remain active. Public sources and archived company websites provide evidence on company formation, technology fields and geography, alongside acquisitions, closures, valuations and involvement in artificial intelligence, defence and space. Company formation continued beyond the apparent 2018 peak in the earlier study. Computing software and applications remain the largest field, with suppliers and supporting businesses accounting for almost a third of active companies. Countries with similar company totals can have different technological profiles, and regional comparisons reveal concentrations obscured by country rankings. The first companies generally preceded the selected national policy milestones. Supporting businesses usually followed technical companies in the same jurisdiction. AI is more prevalent than defence in current company activities, while defence shows the larger increase from the earliest assessed evidence. Space relevance is documented for more than a quarter of active companies, often alongside defence involvement.

papers.title: Influence of Assortativity on the SICP Spreading Process in Hypergraphs
papers.abstract: Many real-world systems involve group interactions that cannot be captured by pairwise graphs. They can be better represented by hypergraphs where each hyperedge could connect an arbitrary number of nodes. The Susceptible-Infected Contact Process (SICP) has been proposed to model the spreading of information and epidemics on hypergraphs. However, how higher-order topological properties of a hypergraph influence the SICP spreading process remains understudied. In this paper, we examine the impact of hypergraph assortativity based on the Neighborhood Coefficient (NC)-the average size of hyperedges incident to a node-on the SICP spreading process. By introducing a low-complexity measure of hypergraph assortativity grounded in analysis of variance, we apply hyperdegree-preserving rewirings to real-world networks and synthetic hypergraph models to tune their assortativity. We find and explain why lower NC assortativity yields higher average epidemic prevalence and lower prevalence variance across different seed selections. This phenomenon is evident when hyperdegree-preserving rewirings are applied to real-world networks with heterogeneous topological structures, but it is largely absent when comparing synthetic random hypergraphs to their rewired counterparts.

papers.title: Unequal Rewards and the Direction of Scientific Work: Evidence from U.S. Public Universities
papers.abstract: Research on pay dispersion has long asked whether unequal rewards increase or depress performance. Tournament theory expects stronger effort, while social comparison accounts expect withdrawal. Both perspectives, however, treat performance as a single scale on which workers can be ranked. Scientific work often resists such ordering. Some contributions extend recognized lines of inquiry and can be evaluated against prevailing standards; others revise the frames through which value is judged and become legible only later. We argue that intellectual tournaments more readily reward the first kind of contribution than the second. Pay dispersion may therefore be associated not only with how much scholars produce but also with what kinds of intellectual exploration are encouraged. We test this argument with administrative payroll records for 105,050 tenure-line faculty in 4,839 departments at 93 U.S. public universities from 2004 to 2026, linked to publication histories in OpenAlex. For each department, we estimate a separate pay equation using rank, contract basis, and seniority, then measure the Gini of the salary variation this local ladder cannot explain. Scholars in departments with greater unexplained pay dispersion publish more papers and receive more citations, but their work is less disruptive, less novel, and more conventional. Additional analyses show that compensation premiums above the ladder go disproportionately to scholars with broad collaborations and topical breadth. Although the design cannot fully separate treatment from selection, the evidence shows that inequality is not only a distributional outcome but also an evaluative structure, shaping which forms of knowledge are recognized, rewarded, and reproduced within organizations and communities.

papers.title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
papers.abstract: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.
